section.title: The Last Supper
section.sectionRationale: As Passover nears and Satan enters Judas, Jesus gathers His apostles for a meal He has longed to share. He takes bread and cup and gives them a new meaning: this is My body given for you, this cup is the new covenant in My blood poured out for you. At the very table where He gives Himself, a betrayer's hand rests and a quarrel over greatness breaks out, so He redefines greatness as service and promises His own a kingdom. He foretells Peter's denial and His own numbering with transgressors, showing that His death is the fulfillment of Scripture and the ground of a new covenant.
section.thesis: At the Passover table Jesus reveals His death as the sacrifice that seals a new covenant, His body given and His blood poured out for His people, and He calls those who share His meal to greatness through service and to perseverance through His intercession.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the plot and Judas's betrayal; the preparation and institution of the Supper; the dispute over greatness and the promise of the kingdom; and the prediction of Peter's denial with the word about the two swords.

verses.text: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover, was approaching,
and the chief priests and scribes were looking for a way to put Jesus to death, for they feared the people.
Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve.
And Judas went to discuss with the chief priests and temple officers how he might betray Jesus to them.
They were delighted and agreed to give him money.
Judas consented, and began to look for an opportunity to betray Jesus to them in the absence of a crowd.

units.label: The institution of the Supper
units.note: this is My body, given for you

verses.text: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread on which the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed.
Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and make preparations for us to eat the Passover.”
“Where do You want us to prepare it?” they asked.
He answered, “When you enter the city, a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him to the house he enters,
and say to the owner of that house, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’
And he will show you a large upper room, already furnished. Make preparations there.”
So they went and found it just as Jesus had told them. And they prepared the Passover.
When the hour had come, Jesus reclined at the table with His apostles.
And He said to them, “I have eagerly desired to eat this {{pascha|Passover}} with you before My suffering.
For I tell you that I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.”
After taking the cup, He gave thanks and said, “Take this and divide it among yourselves.
For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes.”
And He took the bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is My body, given for you; do this in {{anamnesis|remembrance}} of Me.”
In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new {{diatheke|covenant}} in My blood, which is poured out for you.
Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table.
Indeed, the Son of Man will go as it has been determined, but woe to that man who betrays Him.”
Then they began to question among themselves which of them was going to do this.

units.label: Greatness through service and the promised kingdom
units.note: I am among you as one who serves

verses.text: A dispute also arose among the disciples as to which of them should be considered the greatest.
So Jesus declared, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors.
But you shall not be like them. Instead, the greatest among you should be like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves.
For who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who {{diakoneo|serves}}.
You are the ones who have stood by Me in My trials.
And I bestow on you a kingdom, just as My Father has bestowed one on Me,
so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom and sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

units.label: Peter's denial foretold and the two swords
units.note: I have prayed for you, that your faith will not fail

verses.text: Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you like wheat.
But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”
“Lord,” said Peter, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.”
But Jesus replied, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.”
Then Jesus asked them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” “Nothing,” they answered.
“Now, however,” He told them, “the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag; and the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one.
For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment.”
So they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” “That is enough,” He answered.

pascha.gloss: Passover, the feast recalling Israel's rescue from Egypt by the blood of the lamb. Jesus eagerly desires to eat this Passover, and then transforms it: He is the true Passover Lamb whose blood delivers His people, and the meal now points forward to its fulfillment in the kingdom of God.

anamnesis.gloss: Remembrance, a calling to mind that makes the past present. Do this in remembrance of Me is more than nostalgia; the Supper proclaims and applies afresh the once-for-all death of Christ, so that His people continually receive its benefits and look ahead to His return.

diatheke.gloss: Covenant, a binding arrangement God establishes. Jesus names the cup the new covenant in His blood, fulfilling Jeremiah's promise of a covenant of forgiven sins and changed hearts. The new covenant is sealed not with the blood of animals but with the poured-out blood of the Son.

diakoneo.gloss: To serve, to wait on others, to minister. Against the disciples' quarrel over greatness, Jesus points to Himself: I am among you as one who serves. True greatness in His kingdom is measured by lowly service, the pattern of the Lord who serves His people to the point of laying down His life.

basic.context: Passover approaches, and the leaders look for a way to kill Jesus. Satan enters Judas, who agrees to betray Him for money. Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the meal, and gathers with His apostles, saying He has eagerly longed to eat this Passover before He suffers. He takes bread and cup and gives them new meaning: this is My body, given for you; this cup is the new covenant in My blood, poured out for you. Even as He gives Himself, He points out that the betrayer's hand is on the table. When the disciples argue over who is greatest, He teaches that greatness is service, for He Himself is among them as one who serves, and He promises them a kingdom and thrones. He warns Peter that Satan will sift him, but that He has prayed for him, and foretells his threefold denial. Finally He speaks of buying a sword, showing that He is about to be numbered with transgressors.
basic.hermeneutics: The Supper is the interpretive key: Jesus explains His approaching death as a Passover sacrifice that seals a new covenant, His body and blood given for His people. Around this center Luke places the betrayal, the dispute over greatness, and Peter's denial, all showing that the new covenant community is formed not by human strength but by the self-giving of Christ and His intercession.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus longs to eat the pascha, the Passover, and transforms it around Himself. He commands the Supper as an anamnesis, a remembrance that makes His death ever-present to faith. The cup is the new diatheke, covenant, in His blood. And He defines greatness by pointing to Himself as the one who diakoneo, serves.
basic.typology: The Passover lamb whose blood spared Israel points to Christ, the true Lamb given for His people. The new covenant fulfills Jeremiah's promise of forgiven sins. The numbering with transgressors fulfills Isaiah's suffering servant, who was counted among sinners and bore their sin.
basic.christ: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, the host who gives His own body and blood, and the servant King who is among His people as one who serves. He is the suffering servant numbered with transgressors, and the risen Lord who prays for Peter and bestows a kingdom on His own.
basic.god: God's saving purpose stands sovereign even over betrayal, for the Son of Man goes as it has been determined. God establishes a new covenant of forgiveness in the blood of His Son, and He bestows a kingdom on the lowly who serve. His grace upholds failing disciples through the intercession of Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12 institutes the Passover with the lamb's blood. Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant of forgiven sins. Isaiah 53 foretells the servant numbered with transgressors. 1 Corinthians 11 hands on the words of institution to the church.
basic.oneStory: At the Passover table the whole story of redemption gathers to a point: the true Lamb gives Himself to seal a new covenant of forgiveness. The Supper looks back to Egypt and forward to the kingdom feast, and it forms a people who share Christ's meal, follow His path of service, and are kept by His prayer until they eat and drink at His table in His kingdom.

context.literary:
Luke 22 opens with an interlocking of plots. Verses 1 to 6 put the leaders' fear of the people beside Satan's entry into Judas, and verses 7 to 13 then set a second, quieter plan beside them: the arrangements for the meal, with every detail foretold and found 'just as Jesus had told them,' verse 13. One plot is hatched in secret by men; the other is carried out by a Teacher who knows where the jug-carrier will be. Luke wants the reader to feel which of the two is in charge.

The table scene is built on a rhythm of cup, bread, cup. Luke alone has a cup before the bread, verses 17 and 18, and then a cup after supper, verse 20. The first is tied to a vow about the kingdom, the second to the new covenant, so the meal looks both forward and inward. The betrayer is named after the words of institution, verses 21 and 22, not before, so the reader hears the gift first and the shadow second. A BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts end verse 19 after 'This is My body' and omit verse 20, a textual question that does not alter the longer reading's agreement with 1 Corinthians 11:24 to 25.

After the supper Luke gathers a table talk in four parts: the quarrel over greatness, verses 24 to 27, the promise of the kingdom, verses 28 to 30, the warning to Simon, verses 31 to 34, and the word about purse, bag and sword, verses 35 to 38. Each opens with a failure of the disciples and answers it with something Jesus does for them. They argue; He serves. They are about to be sifted; He has prayed. They will be afraid; He reminds them of Scripture.

The whole scene closes with a note of dullness, 'That is enough,' verse 38, and the narrative moves out to the mount. The upper room is Luke's one long speech by Jesus before the cross and is the first spoken commentary on it.
context.historical:
The Passover meal belonged to the evening that began the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when the lamb was killed at the temple in the afternoon, verse 7, and eaten in Jerusalem with unleavened bread, bitter herbs and cups of wine. Deuteronomy 16:2 and 16:6 require the sacrifice at the place God would choose, which is why the disciples must find a room inside the city. A man carrying a jug of water would stand out, since carrying water is generally thought to have been women's work, which would make it an easy sign to follow. The large upper room, 'already furnished,' would be the kind of guest room that pilgrims rented or borrowed during the feast.

The meal pattern is important. At the Passover table the head of the household blessed the cup, explained the meaning of the unleavened bread and told the story of the exodus in answer to the children's questions, as Exodus 12:26 to 27 provides. Jesus takes this familiar script and puts Himself at the centre of it. The words 'body' and 'blood' set side by side would have called to mind sacrifice, because body and blood were separated in the sacrificial animal, and 'the blood of the covenant' from Exodus 24:8 would have been heard in 'new covenant in My blood.'

The apostles reclined, verse 14, and the places of honour at a banquet were a real matter of rank. A dispute 'as to which of them would be considered the greatest' is not an odd intrusion, because seating at table announced status. Gentile rulers called themselves 'benefactors,' verse 25, and the title was used by Hellenistic kings and Roman patrons for those who gave public gifts, so Jesus is naming a political style that every first hearer would recognise.

Peter's boast about prison and death would not sound hollow in that world, since arrests of troublemakers were common in the festival crowds. The rooster's crowing named a part of the night, and a swords-and-purses scene fits a setting in which travellers carried small blades for protection.
context.canonical:
The Last Supper is a meeting point for four Old Testament streams, and Luke lets each be heard. First the Passover of Exodus 12, in which the lamb's blood on the doorposts sets Israel apart when God passes through Egypt, Exodus 12:13, and the day becomes 'a memorial for you,' Exodus 12:14. Jesus' command 'do this in remembrance of Me' borrows that idea of a memorial. Second, the covenant meal of Sinai, where Moses sprinkles the people and says 'This is the blood of the covenant,' Exodus 24:8. Third, Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, with law written on the heart and sins forgiven and remembered no more, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34. Fourth, the Servant of Isaiah 53, who 'was numbered with the transgressors' and 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, a text Jesus quotes in verse 37.

The New Testament passes the words on at once. Paul writes, 'For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you,' 1 Corinthians 11:23, and gives an almost identical form, adding that every time the church eats and drinks, 'you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes,' verse 26. He calls the bread and cup a 'participation' in the body and blood, and says that the many are 'one body' because they share one loaf, 1 Corinthians 10:16 to 17. He also calls Christ 'our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. Hebrews describes Jesus as 'mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 9:15, with a priest who offered 'one sacrifice for sins' for all time, Hebrews 10:12.

The meal looks forward as well. Jesus says He will not drink the fruit of the vine until the kingdom comes, verse 18, and Revelation 19:9 pronounces blessed 'those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.' The disciples will eat at His table in His kingdom, verse 30. The breaking of bread continues in the life of the early church, Acts 2:42, and on the road to Emmaus the risen Lord is made known when He takes bread, blesses and breaks it, Luke 24:30.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke was writing for a community that already broke bread together, and he wanted them to know what they were doing. The Supper was not an invention of the church but the last act of Jesus before His arrest, and Luke records it so that every later meal can be traced to a particular night, a particular table and a particular promise. The core of his purpose is to make the cross intelligible beforehand. Before any soldier touches Jesus, He has already said what His death means: it is for you, it is a covenant, it is poured out.

Luke also wanted his readers to see that the table does not remove the church's weakness but is given in the midst of it. The betrayer reclines at the table, the disciples quarrel over rank, and Peter is about to fall. A community that expected a flawless fellowship would be shocked by this picture, but Luke gives it as a corrective. The Supper does not belong to the strong; it belongs to those whom Jesus has prayed for and who are asked to be servants.

Finally he wanted them to hear greatness redefined. Within the very scene where Christ gives His body, He says, 'I am among you as one who serves.' The service is not a decoration on His kingship but the manner of it, and His followers are meant to see that the table is where He teaches the pattern they are to live by.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Two things in this chapter are commanded. Jesus tells them to 'do this in remembrance of Me,' verse 19, and the church has taken this as a standing ordinance, as Paul reports it, 1 Corinthians 11:24 to 26. And Jesus tells them that greatness among them should look like the youngest and the servant, verse 26. These are instructions for His people in every age.

Much else is simply recorded. That Jesus held the meal in an upper room, that He reclined at table, that there were two cups, that the meal fell on the evening of Passover, are historical facts and not rules for how every church must arrange its worship. The question of how often the Supper should be taken, what kind of bread, and who may preside is not settled by the narrative. The early church seems to have broken bread frequently, Acts 2:42, but Luke does not give a schedule.

The warning to Simon and the oddly puzzling command about the sword are descriptive of that night's circumstances. Jesus does not say that every disciple must carry a purse or arm himself. The denial of Peter is recorded as a warning and not a pattern, and so is the quarrel at table. The mix is meant to teach us how to read: where a verse gives a command, hear it, and where a verse reports a failure, learn from it without copying it.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by 'This is My body' and 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood'?

views.label: A covenant sign that truly conveys His self-giving death
views.case: The bread and cup are given their meaning by Jesus' words: His body given and His blood poured out for His people, sealing the new covenant of Jeremiah. The Supper is a covenant meal that proclaims and applies His atoning death, so that those who receive it in faith share its benefits.

views.label: A memorial that proclaims His death until He comes
views.case: The stress on 'in remembrance of Me' and the forward look to the kingdom frame the Supper as a proclaiming remembrance, a covenant sign pointing to the once-for-all sacrifice rather than repeating it. It unites the church with Christ's death by faith as it awaits His return.

debates.bearing: Christians differ on how Christ is present, but agree that the Supper is the covenant meal of His people, proclaiming His body given and His blood shed for the forgiveness of sins and binding them to Him until He comes.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean about buying a sword?

views.label: A vivid warning of coming hostility, not a call to arms
views.case: Jesus links the sword to being 'numbered with transgressors' and, when they produce two swords, says 'that is enough', then rebukes their actual use of the sword at His arrest. The saying dramatizes the danger and rejection about to fall on Him and His followers, not a literal command to fight.

views.label: A real, if limited, provision for self-defense in a hostile world
views.case: Some take the instruction more literally as acknowledging that the disciples enter a season of danger and hardship, contrasting the earlier peaceful mission. Yet even so it is bounded, for Jesus heals the wounded servant and forbids further violence.

debates.bearing: Either way Jesus is not authorizing the cause of the kingdom to advance by the sword; He heals His captor's servant and goes willingly to fulfill the Scripture, showing His path is suffering, not force.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 15 opens with a construction that English softens. Jesus says epithymia epethymesa, literally 'with desire I have desired,' a noun joined to its own verb for emphasis, which is a very Hebrew-sounding way of speaking. The BSB gives it as 'I have eagerly desired.' The verb is epithymeo, which can name a good longing or a bad one, and here it names the best kind: He is wanting this meal with all His heart. Notice that the verse speaks of the desire before the suffering, so the cross is not something He endures with reluctance at the table.

In verses 17 and 19 Jesus 'gave thanks,' from eucharisteo. The word is the root of the church's name for the Supper, the Eucharist, and it carries the plain sense of giving thanks. The bread is described as 'given for you,' didomenon hyper hymon, a present participle in the passive, so the giving is presented as something steadily taking place, and hyper, 'for' or 'on behalf of,' is the preposition of substitution and benefit used in the rest of the New Testament of Christ's death.

Verse 20 has a grammar point that careful readers have noticed for a long time. The words 'poured out for you,' to ekchynnomenon, are a participle in the nominative case, which means that grammatically they agree with 'the cup' and not with 'the blood,' which is in the dative. The Greek therefore speaks of the cup being poured out. It is a compressed expression: the cup stands for its contents, and the contents stand for His life. The verb ekcheo is the ordinary word for pouring out blood, and Isaiah 53:12 in the BSB likewise says the Servant 'poured out His life unto death.'

Verse 29 uses a verb that does not show up in the English. 'I bestow on you a kingdom' is kago diatithemai hymin basileian, using diatithemai, the verb that is the cousin of diatheke, covenant, in verse 20. In effect Jesus covenants a kingdom to them as the Father has covenanted one to Him. The new covenant of verse 20 and the kingdom of verse 29 are one gift, and the Greek keeps them in the same family. The word 'trials' in verse 28 is peirasmois, the same root as 'temptation,' and the apostles are those who have 'stood by' Him in them, a perfect participle of diameno, remaining through.

In verse 25 the kings are called 'benefactors,' euergetai, an honorific title. In verse 26 the leader is to be 'like the one who serves,' ho diakonon, the participle of the word the basic study notes. Jesus' own line, 'I am among you as one who serves,' puts the verb in the present tense, so the service is His character and not a single act.

The words to Peter in verses 31 and 32 are full of small marks. 'Satan has asked' translates exetesato, a verb that means to demand or ask for permission, much as Satan asks in Job 1:9 to 12. And 'you' is plural in verse 31, 'to sift all of you,' but singular in verse 32, 'I have prayed for you, Simon.' The prayer is for one man, the danger is for all, and so Peter is made responsible for strengthening the rest. The verb 'fail' in 'your faith will not fail' is a word for eclipse or running out, as of a light. And 'turned back,' epistrepsas, is the ordinary verb of repentance and return, spoken before the fall as if it were already certain.

Finally 'That is enough' in verse 38 is hikanon estin, which can close a conversation on a note of weariness or impatience, as with the LORD's 'That is enough' to Moses in Deuteronomy 3:26. It need not mean that two swords are adequate.

typology.type: The Passover lamb, Exodus 12 and Luke 22:7 to 20
typology.fulfillment: At Passover the lamb's blood on the doorposts turned away judgment, and the meal was kept as a memorial, Exodus 12:13 and 12:14. Jesus eats the meal on the very day the lambs are killed, verse 7, and reads it about Himself: His body given, His blood poured out. Paul puts it directly, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The escalation is great. The lamb protected one household for one night; Christ's blood delivers people from every nation from the judgment due to sin. The type falls short because animals could not remove sin, as Hebrews 10:4 explains, and had to be offered again and again.

typology.type: The blood of the covenant at Sinai, Exodus 24:8
typology.fulfillment: After Israel's promise of obedience, Moses took the blood and sprinkled the people, saying 'This is the blood of the covenant.' Jesus' phrase 'new covenant in My blood' deliberately echoes this and also reaches for Jeremiah 31:31. The old covenant was sealed with animal blood and broken by the people, Jeremiah 31:32. The new covenant is sealed with the blood of the Son and carries its own empowerment, a law written on the heart and sins forgiven, Jeremiah 31:33 to 34. Hebrews 9:15 names Christ the mediator of this covenant. The type is outdone because the first covenant depended on a people who failed, while the second depends on a Mediator who does not.

typology.type: The Servant numbered with transgressors, Isaiah 53:12
typology.fulfillment: Jesus tells the apostles that this Scripture 'must be fulfilled in Me,' verse 37, and the very next scene shows Him taken as if He were an outlaw, verse 52. Isaiah's Servant 'poured out His life unto death' and 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, so the quotation reaches well beyond the label 'criminal' to the entire work of substitution. The pattern in Israel's story is the righteous sufferer who is counted with the guilty. In Christ the guilt that is counted is ours, and the righteous one is truly innocent, as Luke will emphasise at the trial. No earlier sufferer could carry the sin of many.

typology.type: The sifting of the faithful, Job 1 and Amos 9:9
typology.fulfillment: Satan 'has asked to sift each of you like wheat,' verse 31. The picture of asking permission recalls Job 1:12, where Satan may act only within the limit God sets. The sieve recalls Amos 9:9, where God Himself shakes Israel 'as grain is sifted in a sieve' and yet 'not a pebble will reach the ground.' The pattern is that God allows testing and sets its bounds, and the faithful are kept. In Christ the bound is guaranteed by a prayer: 'I have prayed for you.' Hebrews 7:25 says that He 'always lives to intercede.' The type falls short only in that Job had no mediator at his side.

study.christ:
The Supper leads to Christ first because He interprets His own death before it happens. No one has yet touched Him, yet He says 'given for you' and 'poured out for you,' as a priest might explain a sacrifice. Luke 24:26 will later tell us that it was 'necessary for the Christ to suffer these things,' and the table shows that He knew it and went willingly. Hebrews 12:2 says He 'endured the cross, scorning its shame,' and verse 15 here discloses the longing that carried Him.

He is the Passover Lamb and the host of the meal at once, which no Old Testament Passover could be. The head of the household led the old meal, but the lamb was another creature. In the upper room the one who gives the bread is the one the bread represents. Paul draws this out when he says that the cup is a 'participation in the blood of Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:16. He is giver and gift.

He is the mediator of the new covenant. Jeremiah promised a covenant in which God would put His law in their minds and 'remember their sins no more,' Jeremiah 31:33 and 31:34. Jesus announces that it begins in His blood. The covenant is not an idea but a person's death, and its benefits, forgiveness, a changed heart, a place in the kingdom, come only through Him. That is why Hebrews calls Him 'mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 9:15.

He is the Servant King. In the same room where kings are described as benefactors, He says, 'I am among you as one who serves.' John records the same night in the foot washing, 'I have set you an example,' John 13:15, and Mark's parallel says the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Greatness is redefined by the person of Christ and not just by His teaching.

He is the praying High Priest. 'I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail.' The same Lord who will soon be silent before accusers speaks for a failing disciple before the Father, and He does it before the failure and not after it. Hebrews 7:25 states the doctrine, 'He always lives to intercede for them,' and Isaiah 53:12 had already said that the Servant 'made intercession for the transgressors.'

He is also the King who bestows a kingdom, verses 29 and 30. The man about to be arrested promises thrones, and promises a feast in His kingdom. The same Jesus who says He will not eat again until the kingdom comes is the one who will lead the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The man with the water jug and the large upper room are details of Luke's narrative and not hidden pictures of the gospel, and the two swords are not an allegory. The weight of the passage lies in what Jesus says about His body, blood and covenant.
study.god:
The passage shows a God whose plan is not threatened by betrayal. Satan enters Judas, the leaders plot, the disciples falter, and yet Jesus says, 'the Son of Man will go as it has been determined,' verse 22. The arrangements for the meal are foretold and fulfilled to the letter, verses 10 to 13. Providence here does not remove the guilt of Judas, for Jesus says 'woe to that man who betrays Him,' but it does mean that the worst thing the human heart does becomes the instrument of the best thing God does. The cross is no accident of history. It was planned, and it was also a crime, and Scripture holds both without apology.

God is a God of covenant. The word runs through the whole passage, from the covenant blood in verse 20 to the covenanted kingdom in verse 29. He binds Himself to a people by promise and by blood, and He does it at His own cost. His faithfulness does not depend on the people's, a point driven home in the same hour by Peter's coming denial. A covenant-keeping God is the only kind who could found a church out of people like these.

He is a God who gives. The bread is 'given for you' and the cup is 'poured out for you,' and the Father bestows a kingdom on the Son and the Son bestows it on His own, verse 29. Even greatness, in this passage, is not seized but given. The generosity of God sits behind the whole scene, so that the Supper is first of all a gift to be received before it is a duty to be performed.

He is a God who holds the powers within bounds. Satan 'has asked' to sift the disciples, which implies that he cannot act without permission, as in Job 1:12. Peter's faith will be tried, but the prayer of the Son ensures that it 'will not fail.' This is a comfort that avoids two errors, treating evil as a rival equal to God and treating it as unreal.

He is holy and just. The woe on the betrayer is real, and the cup of the covenant cost a death. Forgiveness is not cheap. The same God who forgives iniquity and remembers sins no more, Jeremiah 31:34, does so through blood, and the justice of God and the mercy of God meet in the cross.

He is also a God who dwells with His people at a table. Worship here is not remote. It is shared bread and a shared cup, with a promise of the kingdom feast, and it is shaped by gratitude, as the repeated 'gave thanks' shows. The fitting response is to receive with thanks, to remember, to serve one another as He served, and to wait for the day He drinks the cup new with His people.

crossReferences.note: The Passover instructions: the lamb's blood on the houses so that judgment passes over, and the day made 'a memorial.' Jesus eats this meal and reinterprets it, so the lamb, the blood and the memorial all find their meaning in Him. The idea of a memorial stands behind 'in remembrance of Me.'

Moses sprinkles the covenant blood on the people: 'This is the blood of the covenant.' The phrase is close to Jesus' own words over the cup and shows that He is sealing a covenant, with sacrificial blood, in the manner of Sinai but with a better blood.

The promise of a new covenant, unlike the one the fathers broke, with God's law inscribed on the heart and sins remembered no more. Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 both use Jeremiah's own phrase 'new covenant,' so Jeremiah is the horizon of the whole Supper.

The Servant 'was numbered with the transgressors' and 'made intercession for the transgressors.' Jesus quotes the first phrase in verse 37 and acts out the second in verse 32, where He prays for Simon. Both halves of the verse are fulfilled in one night.

Paul hands on the same words of institution that he 'received from the Lord' and adds that the church 'proclaims the Lord's death until He comes.' It confirms that Luke's account is the shared tradition of the early church, and shows that the meal looks forward to His return.

'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' Paul names what the upper room implies. Luke does not use the title, but he places Jesus' words at the exact hour when lambs were being killed, so the two testimonies agree.

Jesus teaches that rulers of the Gentiles lord it over others but among His followers the great must be servants, because the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many.' It is the same lesson as Luke 22:25 to 27, with its theological ground stated.

On the same night John records that Jesus washed the disciples' feet and said 'I have set you an example.' It shows what 'one who serves' looked like in practice and fills the gap in Luke, who gives the saying but not the basin.

Satan appears before the LORD and may touch Job's goods only within a limit: 'Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself.' This explains the shape of Luke 22:31, where Satan has to ask before he sifts.

The Son 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near. The prayer for Simon in verse 32 is a sample of this ongoing work, and the chapter in Hebrews shows why a fallen disciple can still be sure of being kept.

The 'marriage supper of the Lamb' fulfils the promise in verses 16 and 18 that He will eat and drink again in the kingdom. The upper room is the last table before the cross and the first table of a series that ends in the final feast.

At Emmaus the risen Lord takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it, and the disciples recognise Him. The four verbs echo Luke 22:19, and suggest that the breaking of bread is where the risen Christ is known in the life of the church.

study.oneStory:
The Supper answers two questions the story has carried since Egypt. How can God dwell with a people who keep breaking His covenant? And what will it take to deal with the sin that the sacrifices could only point to? From the first Passover onward the pattern is blood and deliverance, and from Sinai onward the pattern is covenant and failure. Jeremiah saw that the failure needed a deeper answer than a new set of rules, and promised a covenant that would do what the old one could not.

On this night the story reaches its hinge. Jesus takes the oldest meal of Israel and says that its meaning has arrived. The lamb, the blood and the memorial are gathered into His body and blood, and the covenant that Jeremiah promised begins. Behind it lies the larger drama, since Satan's entry into Judas and the request to sift the apostles belong to the long conflict that began in the garden, Genesis 3, and that Jesus has already met in the wilderness, when the devil left Him 'until an opportune time,' Luke 4:13. The hour has come.

The scene also sets up what follows. The prayer for Peter anticipates the denial and the restoration. The word about being numbered with transgressors sets up the arrest and the cross. The promise of thrones for the Twelve points to the church of Acts, where the apostles teach and lead, and ultimately to the renewal of all things in which the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, Matthew 19:28. The meal that the church keeps ever since carries the new covenant into every place and century, and Paul says that it proclaims the Lord's death 'until He comes.'

In the new creation the table is set again. Jesus said He would not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes, and Revelation sees a feast, the marriage supper of the Lamb. The story that began with a meal and a forbidden fruit in a garden ends with a meal given freely at the Lamb's own table. The people who share it are those who were kept by His prayer and covered by His blood, and who have learned from Him what greatness is.

quiz.q: What new meaning does Jesus give to the bread and the cup?

options.text: His body given for them and the cup as the new covenant in His blood, poured out for them.
options.note: Luke 22:19-20 gives the body given and the new covenant in His blood.

options.text: A remembrance of His coming death for His disciples.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific new covenant sealed in His poured-out blood.

options.text: A continuation of the old Passover unchanged.
options.note: He transforms the Passover around Himself, instituting something new.

options.text: A symbol with no connection to His death.
options.note: The bread and cup point directly to His body given and blood poured out.

quiz.q: How does Jesus redefine greatness when the disciples argue about it?

options.text: The greatest should be like the youngest and the leader like one who serves, as He is among them as one who serves.
options.note: Luke 22:26-27 grounds greatness in service, modeled by Jesus Himself.

options.text: The greatest among them must serve the others.
options.note: True, but it omits that Jesus points to Himself as the serving one who defines the pattern.

options.text: Greatness comes from having authority over others.
options.note: That is the way of the Gentile kings, which Jesus tells them not to imitate.

options.text: They should stop caring about the kingdom altogether.
options.note: Jesus bestows a kingdom on them; He redirects greatness, not the kingdom.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say to Simon Peter about his coming trial?

options.text: That Satan asked to sift him, but Jesus has prayed that his faith will not fail, and he must later strengthen his brothers.
options.note: Luke 22:31-32 shows Satan's request, Jesus' intercession, and the call to strengthen others.

options.text: That He has prayed for Peter so his faith will not fail.
options.note: True and central, but it omits Satan's sifting and the call to strengthen the brothers afterward.

options.text: That Peter is strong enough to withstand the coming test.
options.note: Jesus foretells Peter's denial; his keeping rests on Christ's prayer, not his own strength.

options.text: That Peter will never be shaken at all.
options.note: Jesus foretells that Peter will deny Him three times.

quiz.q: What does Jesus reveal about His death when He speaks of the two swords and Scripture?

options.text: That He must be numbered with the transgressors, fulfilling what is written about Him.
options.note: Luke 22:37 cites Isaiah 53:12: He was numbered with transgressors.

options.text: That difficult and dangerous days were coming for His followers.
options.note: True of the context, but the stated point is the fulfillment of Scripture in His being counted a criminal.

options.text: That the disciples should arm themselves to defend the kingdom.
options.note: He rejects the use of the sword at His arrest; the saying dramatizes rejection, not armed defense.

options.text: That He would escape His enemies by force.
options.note: He goes willingly to fulfill Scripture, not to fight His way free.

quiz.q: How does Luke show that God's purpose stands even over the betrayal?

options.text: Jesus says the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, even as woe falls on the betrayer.
options.note: Luke 22:22 holds together divine determination and human responsibility.

options.text: Jesus knows in advance that Judas will betray Him.
options.note: True, but it omits that His going is according to God's determined plan, not mere foreknowledge.

options.text: God forces Judas to betray Jesus against his will.
options.note: Judas acts willingly and is held guilty; God's purpose stands without excusing him.

options.text: The betrayal takes God by surprise and derails His plan.
options.note: The opposite: the Son of Man goes exactly as it was determined.

questions: Jesus said He eagerly desired to share this meal before He suffered. How does it move you to know that His heart was set on giving Himself for you?
The Supper is a remembrance that proclaims His body given and blood poured out. When you take the bread and cup, are you receiving them as more than ritual, as Christ's own self-giving for you?
At the table where Jesus gave Himself, the disciples argued about who was greatest. Where does the hunger for status still creep into your following of a Lord who serves?
Jesus told Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith will not fail. How does it steady you to know that your perseverance rests on Christ's intercession and not on your own strength?
When Peter is restored he is to strengthen his brothers. How might God want to use your own failures and restorations to strengthen others?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts end verse 19 after 'This is My body' and omit the words that follow, including verse 20. The BSB includes the longer, well-attested text with the second cup and the new covenant saying, which agrees with Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12, 'And He was numbered with the transgressors', applying the suffering servant prophecy directly to Himself as He goes to be arrested and executed among criminals.

The instruction to buy a sword, followed by 'That is enough', is best read as a vivid warning of coming hostility rather than a call to arms, since Jesus heals the servant wounded at His arrest and forbids further violence.
